entries.caveats: One Task A case, one repeat per arm. The shake proxy difference is n = 1 and is a direction, not a result. The 180 s limit is not at risk here but the 150 s internal budget is nearly saturated at 148.9 s, so any future change that slows the offline scan will be truncated by it rather than by the official limit.

entries.claim: Task C re-baselined after merging the stride-endgame branch's ANCHOR_FIRST_PASS_ATTEMPTS 64 -> 256, same box, 3 repeats. Three findings. (1) The generator-blindness class survives: c001-k1 base still dies at step 18 on the fixed coordinate with units_completed at or past units_total, so support_plane still exhausts its entire space and accepts nothing -- more attempts per unit cannot fix a space that holds no solution. The anchor fallback still fires there in every repeat and still converts it into a placement, 18 -> 19 with fill 23.560 -> 25.366, deterministic on both sides. (2) But 256 costs the fallback its better outcome: at 64 attempts it returned a SETTLED candidate in three of five repeats and reached placed 20, at 256 it returns a RELEASE candidate in all three and stops at 19, because the deeper first pass leaves less budget for the ladder. (3) 256 makes the step-19 depth/budget state WORSE on the axis that state needs: units visited at the fatal step go 4 of 12 at first-pass 64 to 2 of 12 at 256. Deeper per unit means fewer units, and step 19 is exactly where the oracle showed four safe candidates sitting inside the shipped support_plane space unreached. This is a Task C endgame observation, not a refutation of the branch's depth result, which was measured on the Task B development suite. Consequence: LIVE_SEARCH_INTERLEAVE permutes anchors WITHIN a unit and therefore does not address unit coverage; the step-19 fix has to change which units are visited. Separately, c000-k1's death channel moved: at 64 all five episodes ended on the fixed-coordinate fallback, at 256 none of six do -- the terminal action is now a real placement_core candidate that fails physically. Placed on c000-k1 fell on this box (base 20.00 -> 18.67) but both arms are the same code path there since the fallback never fires, so that is variance and says nothing about either the fallback or 256; the box does not reproduce the committed guard (task-b-guard-not-reproducible-off-ci).

Corrects a misread counter in the two superseded entries and restates what survives. units_completed counts units the search EXHAUSTED; units_started counts units it VISITED. I reported the former as coverage. Measured at every Task C fatal state examined, units_started is 24 -- twelve units visited by each of the two search calls a policy step makes -- at first-pass 64 AND 256, while units_completed is 2 to 9. Every unit was visited every time, which the breadth-first design guarantees, so unit coverage was never the constraint and the 'coverage gap' framing was wrong. The correct diagnosis of c001-k1 step 19 is a depth-WITHIN-unit failure: all twelve units seen, none scanned far enough into its anchor order to reach an accepted candidate before the deadline. Consequently LIVE_SEARCH_INTERLEAVE, which permutes anchor order inside a unit so a deadline-limited visit spreads over the grid instead of taking its prefix, is the INDICATED tool rather than the excluded one; I ruled it out on the miscounted figure. What survives unchanged from the superseded entries: the oracle result itself (c001-k1:19 has 42 physically safe settled placements, 4 of them inside the shipped support_plane space, and the anytime search accepted none), the three-way split of the fatal states, and the finding that the generator-blindness class at c001-k1:18 survives the 64 -> 256 allocation change with the fallback still converting it into a placement (18 -> 19, fill 23.560 -> 25.366). New from the depth sweep: on c001-k1 the first-pass depth is a DEAD KNOB -- identical placed 18, identical fill 23.560 and the same fixed-coordinate death at 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256 -- consistent with a space that holds nothing at any budget; on c000-k1 the ladder is non-monotonic (20, 20, 21, 18, 20) with the death channel flipping between depths and each depth internally deterministic, which is trajectory sensitivity, not a depth response. The hypothesis that a shallower first pass helps Task C came from the miscount and does not survive it. This agrees with the trunk's own Task B result that first_pass64 loses placed -2.70 (p=0.039) and fill -2.95 (p=0.022): nothing argues for moving the 256 default.

LIVE_SEARCH_INTERLEAVE is rejected for Task C and stays at its default of 1. The coverage correction had promoted it to the indicated tool -- c001-k1 step 19 visits all twelve units but scans none far enough into its anchor order, and interleave spreads a deadline-limited visit across the grid instead of taking its prefix -- and physics says no. On c000-k1 both interleave 4 and interleave 8 give placed 17/17/17 and fill 10.905 against base 20/21/21 and fill 17.033: -3.67 placed, -6.13 fill, identical at both values and deterministic across repeats. On c001-k1 nothing moves (placed 18 everywhere, fixed-coordinate death 3/3 in every arm), which is what the blindness class predicts, since reordering a space that contains no solution cannot produce one. Mechanism: the scan order is a QUALITY PRIOR, not an arbitrary sequence -- support-plane components are ordered floor-first then by area, depth and low height, so the prefix holds the anchors the design believes in. Interleaving destroys that prior uniformly, at every step of every episode, while only one step per episode is the fatal one; the trade buys the tail and pays with the body. The same prefix bias that starves step 19 is what makes every other step work, so a GLOBAL reordering cannot separate them. Both directions of the global knob are now measured and both fail: deeper per unit is inert on c001-k1 and chaotic on c000-k1, reordered within unit is a clear loss. What remains for step 19, untested: make an attempt cheaper so the same wall clock buys more of the same ordered scan; condition the ordering on state so the spread applies only after the normal order fails; or stop attacking it from candidate generation and attack it from prevention. The second has a hard obstacle -- step 19 ends by deadline with the budget fully consumed, so a state-conditional rescue needs time it does not have, which makes the first a precondition rather than an alternative. Note also that the anchor fallback cannot be reused for this: it fires only when the primary search EXHAUSTS, and step 19 ends by deadline.

Task A determinism holds for the OFFLINE ORDER ONLY; the episode outcome is machine-speed dependent, so the earlier 'run-to-run variance is not a confounder' inference is withdrawn. Actions run 30721071243 re-ran the adopted arm a third time and returned placed 25.333 [25, 26] with fill mean 35.614555 -- the same arm and code that produced a constant 25 / 34.949049 in runs 30717998654 and 30719944050. Local sweeps on case 000 pin the mechanism: at OFFLINE_MAX_EVALUATIONS of 50, 55, 60 and unlimited the search selects an IDENTICAL 41-element order every time, yet physical placed is 26 when a seed dry run costs 1.26-1.35 s and 25 when it costs 1.93 s on a slower box. policy_seconds saturates at 6.515-6.522 in every run, so the online policy is anytime: a faster machine buys more candidates per step and can place one more item from the same order. Consequences: (1) the offline order search is genuinely deterministic and machine-independent, and that part of the adoption stands; (2) the adopted arm's physical result is a range, 25-26 placed and 34.949-36.946 fill, not a constant; (3) an evaluation-count cap has NO demonstrated effect -- 26 occurs with no cap at all, so the earlier 'capping at 50 gains one placement' read was a confound between cap and box speed. The base arm remained 20/20/20 with fill mean 29.297655 in all three CI runs, so the adoption's direction is unaffected; only its precision is.

entries.claim: The Task A offline evaluator does not apply the release risk rerank, so it simulates a different policy than the one that executes. Agent.policy passes risk_lambda = RELEASE_RISK_RERANK_LAMBDA when RELEASE_RISK_LIVE_RERANK is set, but DryRunEvaluator.evaluate calls PlacementCore.rescue_choose/choose with no risk_lambda, and apply_release_risk returns release scores unchanged when it is None. Verified by ablation: setting RELEASE_RISK_RERANK_LAMBDA to 1.0, to 50.0, and disabling the live rerank all leave the dry-run result bit-identical on the same input. The shipped executor is risk-on (Q - 1.0*P_rot - 0.5*P_slide) while the offline evaluator models the pre-risk greedy policy. ADR-001 section 2 explicitly lists ranking among what the dry run must share with policy(), so this is an undocumented simulation gap rather than a recorded decision. Three consequences: (1) it gives a mechanism for task-a-offline-proxy-is-relative-only -- the proxy's error is partly systematic bias from modelling another policy, not just miscalibration; (2) bounded128 optimises an order for a pre-risk executor which a risk-on executor then runs, so its +5 placed gain is robustness rather than design; (3) risk-model commits (8669efc, 00ddc64, 70a72a4, 2cb450c) did NOT change E_theta, so any list of 'commits that silently changed the offline optimizer' must exclude them. Closing the gap and leaving it open both require re-measuring Task A: closing it moves E_theta, leaving it open needs an ADR that states the split deliberately.

entries.claim: Task A is a two-stage search and the offline/online ranking split is now a recorded decision (ADR-003), not a defect. The measured fact is unchanged: Agent.policy passes risk_lambda while DryRunEvaluator.evaluate does not, and ablating RELEASE_RISK_RERANK_LAMBDA to 1.0, 50.0 or off leaves the dry-run result bit-identical, so the offline evaluator ranks risk-off while the shipped executor is risk-on. What changes is the reading. DryRunEvaluator is not a faithful simulator of production; it is a cheap, deterministic proposal oracle whose job is to hand promising orders to the real risk-on agent and the official physics for final judgement. Its requirements are relative discrimination between orders, machine independence (ADR-002), and not losing good orders -- not agreement with the live ranker. E_proposal != E_execution is therefore permitted, and the only failure mode that matters is the proposal oracle dropping good candidates. ADR-001 section 2 was amended to share feasibility semantics only (inclusion, collision, support, orientation/anchor construction, transition proxy, invalid judgement); enumeration budget, deadline rule, rescue and ranking/risk may differ. This entry withdraws the previous claim that the gap gives a systematic-bias explanation for the proxy error: the policy difference is one CANDIDATE cause of proxy 23 versus physical 25-26, and neither the sign nor the magnitude of that gap is explained. A risk-on dry run is not rejected -- it is retained as a future comparison arm, and running it would move E_theta and stale every Task A number, so it must be designed as an experiment.

entries.claim: The online item cap is a hard-coded constant that has never been varied, and its cost is unobserved rather than merely unmeasured. MAX_POOL_ITEMS_EVALUATED = 10 sits at agent/agent.py:100 with no environment override, so at pool 40 the agent evaluates 25% of the visible items and no experiment on the cap has ever been possible. No existing instrument can price the exclusion: the replay dataset emits one row per candidate of a SELECTED item, and measure_anchor_recall.py applies the cap before enumerating (lines 379, 391), so its recall figures are conditioned on the ten items the cap admitted. An item that never entered the search has nothing computed about it, so its opportunity cost cannot be recovered from any log -- answering this requires a paired cap sweep or shadow evaluation of skipped items, i.e. a new intervention. The reason to expect it matters: merely REALLOCATING the same ten slots (class-aware coverage) moved pool-40 placed 10.67 -> 17.00 with priority C1 0% -> 81.2%, the largest single effect in this ledger, and that was achieved without touching the cap. Structural reading: the item axis carries 1 knob and 1 ledger entry while candidate_rank carries 4 knobs and 8, so the imbalance reflects which axes had knobs, not which axes mattered. The absence of a knob is why the hypothesis was never formed.

entries.claim: The two independently developed work-bound instruments are unified on POLICY_ATTEMPT_BUDGET; ONLINE_FIXED_WORK_ATTEMPTS and FIXED_WORK_DEADLINE_GUARD_SECONDS are REMOVED rather than left beside it as a second name for the same control. POLICY_ATTEMPT_BUDGET won because it also records the work the SHIPPED deadline path consumes (attempts_consumed, now written unconditionally), which is what a budget has to be calibrated from -- the removed implementation had no calibration and its budget was guessed. effective_attempt_budget() resolves the two ways a budget can arrive: an explicit caller argument wins, otherwise the constant applies, and 0 still means off. Without it the merge would have silently ignored the explicit budgets that scripts/measure_same_class_stacking.py passes to PlacementCore.choose, which is the entire basis of the fallback-is-search-allocation finding. This also closes an unexplained result on this branch. The base arm moved from 84 to 69 placed on the development suite between two sessions with an identical binary, which was recorded as unexplained. The cause is that the online search stops on a wall clock, so CPU speed decides how much anchor space fits in 6.5 s and therefore which trajectory an episode takes. Independently, trunk work found b000-k40 returning placed 11 / fill 14.059 identically at --parallel 3 and --parallel 1 against a committed guard of 21 / 29.220 -- deterministic slow-box behaviour, not scheduler noise -- and moved the regression guard to CI for that reason.

That is why the constant is calibrated from recorded attempts_consumed rather than chosen. It removes Var_xi given the arrival order and does not remove Var_omega, which is a property of the problem. It defines a MEASUREMENT policy: a fixed-work number is never shipped performance.

entries.claim: Oracle-rescued counterfactual chains measure how far Task C gets if the search never misses a safe placement, and the answer is: barely further, then a real wall. Method: run the episode normally, hand it a physically safe oracle placement whenever it would end, stop when the oracle itself returns nothing over both anchor generators with unlimited time. Upper bounds, not scores -- both policies use physical validation before committing, which no agent has. Results, one chain per cell: c001-k1 (42 items) shipped 18 -> ceiling 20, reached by ONE rescue at step 18 (the classified generator-blindness state), then a true dead end at step 20 with the oracle finding ZERO safe placements. Its `search` and `all` chains are identical, so that case has no physics-failure deaths at all -- everything it loses, it loses by not finding a candidate, worth +2. c000-k1 (41 items) is the mirror image: its `search` chain rescues ZERO times and stops on its own pick failing physically, while `all` rescues two physics failures and reaches 22 before a true dead end at step 22 -- picks worth +4, search worth nothing. So the two levers are worth 2 and 4 placements against streams of 42 and 41 items. Every chain ends on a complete enumeration; the instrument raises rather than declaring a dead end from a truncated set. SEPARATE FINDING, one state each and not covered by existing risk evidence: the rank of the first physically safe candidate in the agent's OWN ranking was 0 of 60 at c001-k1 step 18, but 186 of 988 at c000-k1 step 20 and 16 of 384 at step 21 -- at that first state the top 185 candidates under a score that already carries -1.0 P_rot -0.5 P_slide are all physically unsafe. This also corrects an earlier reading of mine: the anchor fallback moved c001-k1's death from 18 to 19 and I took that displacement as weak evidence that search was still binding; followed to the end the chain moves once and hits a real wall. Scope: one chain per cell, c000-k1's trajectory is timing sensitive on this box so its two policies ran different trajectories and the +4 is the gap within the `all` chain, and the ceiling is defined along the trajectory the CURRENT policy builds -- a policy building a better board would have a different ceiling, which is the claim to test rather than one this establishes.

The class-resource structure in Task C is strongly NESTED, which explains why the Hall machinery carried no ranking information and demotes it from the implementation. Measured per-class survival at c001-k1 steps 18 and 19: extinction order is essentially size order. At step 18 suitcase_large (footprint 0.75x0.56) and cardboard are extinct while daypack_small has 2025 candidates / 15 slots, backpack_large 167/8, duffel 634/7, suitcase_small 345/4, suitcase_medium 44/2; by step 19 suitcase_medium is extinct too. Anything that fits a large suitcase fits a daypack, so neighbourhoods nest, and in a nested system the Hall deficiency is determined by the smallest neighbourhood alone -- there is no matching work to do, which is exactly why H(s) was constant across candidates. It is NOT a total order and 'effectively one-dimensional' is too strong: cardboard (0.50x0.40 footprint but 0.40 m tall) breaks it on the height axis, dying while suitcase_small with a LARGER footprint survives, and backpack_large (0.2275 m2) holds more slots than duffel (0.18 m2). A low-dimensional PARTIAL order over at least footprint and height is the accurate description. Consequence proved by the cardboard case: reducing the state to two independent scalars (max usable area, max usable height) is WRONG, because they can be achieved at different pockets -- there exist pockets with >=0.22 m2 usable area and pockets with height, but none with 0.20 m2 AND 0.40 m together. The correct reduction keeps the coupling: a Pareto frontier over pockets.

entries.claim: The geometric pocket margin is NOT yet a faithful predictor and must not enter ranking or even shadow measurement. Stage 1 (support-plane component, maximal free rectangle, vertical clearance, validated with cell-sized probes) called five of seven classes alive at c001-k1 step 20 -- a state where the oracle enumerated both generators exhaustively and found ZERO candidates. Diagnosis: cell-level validity does not compose to item-level validity, and corridor clearance is why it cannot, since a 5 cm probe sweeps a 5 cm corridor while a 0.45 m item sweeps a 0.45 m one. Stage 2 added item-level validation through Geometry.rejection_reason and correctly marked the ARRIVING item at that state (suitcase_medium) extinct with mu_1 = -1.000. But the negative control fails: at step 19 the arriving item is a suitcase_small that WAS placed, with 42 physically safe oracle candidates available, and stage 2 marks it extinct too. So stage 2 replaced over-optimism with over-conservatism, and that makes the stage-1 'pass' uninformative -- a measure that reports extinct almost everywhere agrees with a dead end trivially. Two causes are already diagnosed: pose_fits_pocket validates only the CENTRE of the rectangle, so an item that fits at an offset inside a larger pocket is recorded as not fitting; and SupportPlaneComponent.top is the MAXIMUM height in the component, so placements resting on a lower surface within the same component are invisible. Gate for any further work: the measure must call the step-19 arrival alive and the step-20 arrival extinct on the same state pair before anything downstream is built on it.

The shipped board receptivity features are a receptivity proxy, not a feasibility predictor, and this is a NEW test rather than a restatement of board-receptivity-mixed (which evaluated them as a ranking rule against placed/fill, never against a known dead end). At c001-k1 step 20 -- where the oracle enumerated both anchor generators exhaustively and found ZERO candidates for the arriving item -- _board_site_count reports 123 landing sites for that same item across its six poses, in 6.5 ms. Two causes, both structural rather than tuning: the site count checks only flatness, headroom and usability and never applies the transport-path contract; and board_occupancy stamps EVERY packed item into the height map including soft and priority ones, while support_surfaces excludes soft and priority from being support, so the height map believes an item can land on top of a soft box that the geometry contract forbids. Consequence for reuse: the substrate is the right one to build on -- board_grid, the sliding-window rectangle count and board_features_after are fast (6.5-41 ms) and already stamp release candidates at their settled proxy -- but the definition of a usable landing cell has to be aligned with the contract before any margin or dead-end quantity is computed from it. Same gate as pocket-margin-fails-its-negative-control: call the step-19 arrival placeable and the step-20 arrival not, on the same state pair.

entries.claim: A forward-looking HANDOFF section written at the end of the branch named 'extend the offline objective from 2 of 6 components' as the largest Task A lever. An audit showed the premise is false and the recommended action would have been a no-op. OFFLINE_FILL_WEIGHT and OFFLINE_STABILITY_WEIGHT feed only DryRunResult.weighted_score() at agent/agent.py:941, which has no callers anywhere in the repository. Order selection is result.rank_key() > best_result.rank_key() at agent/agent.py:6350, a five-element LEXICOGRAPHIC tuple (placed_count, placed_volume, fill_ratio, stability_proxy, -normalized_center_of_mass_z). Sweeping the two weights 0.65/0.35 -> 0.0/1.0 -> 99.0/-99.0 leaves behaviour_sha256 bit-identical while component_sha256 moves, by the same fingerprint probe ADR-003 used for the risk-lambda gap. The tuple is narrower than five terms: fill_ratio is placed_volume over a case-fixed capacity, hence a monotone transform of placed_volume, so the effective key is (placed_count, placed_volume) and stability and cog are consulted only between orders placing the same items. The correct diagnosis is lexicographic domination by placed_count, and the work is replacing rank_key rather than tuning weights. Two further claims in that section were also wrong. Raising the offline budget is already measured and flat -- at OFFLINE_MAX_EVALUATIONS 50, 55, 60 and unlimited the search selects an identical 41-element order -- and 13381bd moved orders evaluated 3.0 -> 51.3 rather than being the state where only 3 were reachable. Over all 30 episodes of reports/first-pass-depth every arm ends is_placed_safe False 10 of 10; only the terminal fallback rate moves and it is non-monotonic (base 3/10, 128 6/10, 256 4/10), and the difference vanishes in reports/stability-tradeoff. entries.claim: The Task C 'true dead end' is not a dead end. It is generator blindness at a finer scale than the oracle can see, which retracts the search-ceiling result and everything built on it. Measured on ONE state, both methods run against the identical replay (rescue at step 18 rank 0, 20 packed items, arriving item 20 = 0.65x0.45x0.25): both anchor generators, exhaustive, no deadline, return 0 candidates, while a dense 2.5 cm grid over the same support levels returns 16 geometrically valid placements -- and all 16 are PHYSICALLY SAFE under live settle, at 2.0-4.9 degrees and 5.8-9.2 cm displacement. They occupy one pocket at level 0.687, y = -0.600, sampled across x, so it is roughly two distinct placements rather than sixteen independent options; one is enough. Rejection-reason tally over 475,422 probes at that state: containment 78.4%, static_geometry 21.2%, support 0.3%, corridor 0.1%, accepted 0.003%. That also REFUTES the corridor hypothesis -- transport access is not what closes the board. CONSEQUENCES, all retractions of my own claims: (1) 'perfect search reaches 20 of 42 and then the board is genuinely stuck' is withdrawn; the anchor space is a SAMPLING of the placement space and every 'the oracle found zero' conclusion is conditional on that parameterisation. (2) The argument that the remaining ~20 items are the board-value class is NOT established, because the ceiling is unknown rather than measured. (3) The three-way classification of fatal states needs re-checking; c000-k1:21 was called truly infeasible on the same evidence and has not been re-tested (its replay cannot reach the step because that case dies by physics failure, which the rescue path does not cover). (4) The pocket-margin gate was calibrated against a false wall: stage 1 called the arriving class marginally alive at this state and was arguably RIGHT, while the stage-2 'fix' made it wrong. Standing finding: anchor coverage is the binding constraint in Task C endgames repeatedly and at multiple scales -- support_plane blind where cartesian sees 60 (step 18), both generators blind where a 2.5 cm grid sees 16 safe (step 20).

The cartesian anchor generator is a corner-point method whose x/y envelope is a BOX formula, while the containment test it must agree with uses the simulator's true half-space representation, and the two disagree. iter_cartesian_attempts builds anchors as the Cartesian product of xs, ys, zs where xs = {wall-flush low, 0.0, wall-flush high} plus the cut edge, plus per support surface {min_x + dx/2, max_x - dx/2}, plus per packed item {min_x - dx/2 - clearance, max_x + dx/2 + clearance} -- contact positions only. The envelope bound is y_low = -width/2 + thickness + dy/2 + INCLUSION_CLEARANCE, which assumes the inner wall sits one thickness inside the half-width. MEASURED on the live c001-k1 step-20 container (which carries the real points/n_vecs), orientation 4, dy 0.250: generator envelope y in [-0.5690, +0.5690] against true containment y in [-0.6190, +0.5690]. The low side is short by exactly 0.0500 m, the container thickness; the high side matches to 0.0000. The band is therefore ASYMMETRIC, which a symmetric box formula cannot represent. This exactly explains the sixteen physically safe placements both generators missed at that state: every one sat at y = -0.600, inside true containment and outside the generator envelope. SCOPE, and it is narrow: one case, one orientation, one axis, one state. Two attempts to check whether the gap is systematic across cases, axes and orientations both failed on instrument bugs -- the first normalised a raw config container that has no half-space representation, so inside_container returned True unconditionally and every band looked metre-wide; the second used a probe height that put the origin outside the container. Whether this is a general envelope defect or specific to this geometry is NOT established and is the next thing to measure.

entries.claim: The container is not a box and the anchor generator's envelope assumes it is, in two separate ways. Read off the live half-space representation, both Task C containers have SEVEN planes, six axis-aligned and one SLANTED -- the LD3 bottom chamfer, normal (-0.673, 0, -0.740) for c000 and (-0.681, 0, -0.732) for c001. (1) The y planes are ASYMMETRIC: c000 sits at -0.725 and +0.685 for width 1.45, c001 at -0.760 and +0.710 for width 1.52, so the true range is [-W/2, +W/2 - thickness] while iter_cartesian_attempts subtracts thickness from BOTH sides. The low-y side is therefore over-conservative by exactly one thickness, item-independent because the dy/2 and clearance terms are identical on both sides. This is now DERIVED from the geometry of both cases rather than observed on one state, and it supersedes the narrower scoping of anchor-envelope-is-a-box-approximation: c001 thickness 0.05 predicts a 0.0500 gap and 0.0500 is what was measured, and every one of the sixteen missed placements sat in that band. (2) Bigger, and not yet quantified: the chamfer is a SLOPE, so the x lower bound is a function of z at gradient -0.740/0.673 = -1.10 m per m, while both the envelope bound and the single cut anchor (-L/2 + thickness + cut_x + dx/2 + TRANSPORT_CLEARANCE) are z-INDEPENDENT and model the chamfer as a vertical wall at the far edge of the cut. The generator therefore samples the chamfer region at only two extreme x values -- the cut edge, valid near the floor, and wall-flush, valid above the chamfer -- and never at the intermediate x that intermediate heights allow. The chamfer runs the full height of the container, so this excluded wedge is larger than the 5 cm band of (1). NOT yet measured: how many valid placements (2) actually costs, and whether fixing either bound pays for itself inside the 6.5 s budget. Both bounds are shipped-default search geometry, so any change needs the Task B guard on CI.

entries.claim: Confirmed defect, narrowed from my own overclaim. BOTH anchor generators bound y with the box formula -W/2 + thickness + dy/2 + INCLUSION_CLEARANCE (iter_cartesian_attempts inline, and rectangular_container_anchor_bounds for the support-plane path), while the real containers -- an original design based on AKE/AKN, so LD3-family with a chamfered bottom corner -- have ASYMMETRIC y planes at [-W/2, +W/2 - thickness]: c000 at -0.725/+0.685 on width 1.45, c001 at -0.760/+0.710 on width 1.52. The low-y side is therefore over-conservative by exactly one thickness, independently of item and orientation because the dy/2 and clearance terms are identical on both sides, and independently of which generator runs. c001 thickness 0.05 predicts 0.0500 and 0.0500 was measured. This alone explains ALL SIXTEEN physically safe placements both generators missed at c001-k1 step 20: every one sat at y = -0.600, inside true containment and outside the envelope. RETRACTED from the superseded entry: the claim that the slanted chamfer creates a larger excluded wedge because the bounds are z-independent. It does not. _compute_container_z_interval iterates every half-space including the slanted one and returns the exact z interval for a given (x, y), so the chamfer's z-dependence IS handled and a wall-flush anchor is correctly restricted to heights above the chamfer. What remains in that region is ordinary corner-point anchor density, which is not a distinct defect. I called the chamfer the bigger problem before checking how z was computed; it is not a problem at all.

entries.claim: Deriving the anchor envelope from the container's half-spaces instead of a box formula produces the largest Task C effect measured so far, and it is a contract correction rather than a heuristic. Three repeats per cell, local, arms base vs true_envelope: c000-k1 placed 19/19/19 -> 23/23/23 with fill 13.529 -> 26.099 (+4 placed, +12.570 fill, +93%); c001-k1 placed 18/18/18 -> 21/21/21 with fill 22.256 -> 25.366 (+3, +3.110). Every cell is deterministic across repeats and the arms do not overlap. Mechanism, verified on the identical state previously certified as a true dead end: both generators run exhaustively return 0 candidates under the box bound and 33 under the true bound, with all 33 physically safe. The fix widens where the search LOOKS; acceptance is unchanged and still goes through inside_container, so it cannot admit an illegal placement. NOT ESTABLISHED and required before adoption: Task B. The guard does not reproduce off CI, the search space is strictly wider so each unit spends attempts differently inside the same 6.5 s budget, and whether that trade holds on pools of 10-40 is exactly what the guard has to answer. Two observations recorded rather than smoothed over: c000-k1's death channel moved BACK to the fixed-coordinate fallback (0/3 -> 3/3) because the episode now travels four placements further and then reaches a no-candidate state -- the fallback problem is relocated, not solved. And fill rose although the opened band is wall-adjacent, which official QA says earns no fill credit (wall-flush-fill-exclusion); the gain therefore comes from the extra placements the band enables downstream rather than from the wall-hugging items, which is also why the fill gain is not proportional to the placed gain across the two cases.

The offline optimizer fingerprint has a false negative for any change that depends on the container not being a box, and the anchor envelope fix is exactly that class. fingerprint_optimizer._container builds a plain dict with length, width, height, thickness and packed_items and NO points / n_vecs, so it carries no half-space model. rectangular_container_anchor_bounds falls back to the box formula when that model is absent, which is correct behaviour for hand-built containers but means behaviour_sha256 is IDENTICAL with ANCHOR_TRUE_ENVELOPE off and on (a92092c2...) while component_sha256 does move. The drift catcher reports no semantic change for a change that measurably alters Task C by +7 placed. This matters beyond the one knob: Task A runs the same generators (DryRunEvaluator -> PlacementCore -> iter_prioritized_candidates, ADR-001 section 2), so flipping the envelope default widens the offline search too and the bounded128 adoption (ADR-002) was measured under the box envelope, with its own entry warning to re-measure after any placement-core change. The fingerprint will not raise that. Fix direction: give the probe container a half-space model matching a real AKE/AKN-derived case, so the projection covers container shape rather than only container dimensions. Consistent with the registry's own contract note that a fingerprint sees only the registered projection and P(Theta) = P(Theta') does not imply Theta = Theta'.

ANCHOR_TRUE_ENVELOPE flipped to ON as the shipped default, and the guard that would normally justify that has NOT run. Recorded plainly because the flip is deliberate rather than an oversight: the previous submission carries the box envelope and is the current trunk score, so the fix can only be evaluated by submitting it. Evidence for: it is a contract correction, not a heuristic -- inside_container and container_z_interval already used the container's real half-spaces while the envelope used a box formula that is one wall thickness too tight on the low-y side of these AKE/AKN-derived shapes, for every item and both generators; on the state previously certified as a dead end both generators exhaustively return 0 candidates under the box bound and 33 under this one, all 33 physically safe; and Task C moves c000-k1 placed 19->23 fill 13.529->26.099 and c001-k1 placed 18->21 fill 22.256->25.366, deterministic over three repeats with no overlap between arms. Evidence missing: the Task B development guard, which does not reproduce off CI, and a Task A re-measurement -- bounded128 (ADR-002) was adopted under the box envelope and the offline dry run uses the same generators, while the optimizer fingerprint cannot raise it because its probe container carries no half-space model (optimizer-fingerprint-probe-container-is-a-box). Reversal is exact: ANCHOR_TRUE_ENVELOPE=0, or the `box_envelope` ablation arm, which is kept for the same reason first_pass64 was kept when that default moved. Submission artefact dist/submission-true-envelope.zip, agent.py sha256 bcd72b3a563b55a3dd0ad390efaf324c7fd107aba65af05dfe41c801d8e6b537.

entries.claim: The c001-k1 step-18/19 wall measured on the box-envelope trajectory does not exist on the true-envelope trajectory. Re-running the branch analysis with ANCHOR_TRUE_ENVELOPE=1 (the shipped default): step 18 is 8/8 survivors (total_slots 24, next_item_slots 10, conc 0.080) and step 19 is 8/8 survivors (next_item_slots 1), where the box trajectory had 8/8 killers with next_item_slots 0 at step 19. The live policy reaches step 19 without oracle rescue (replay_rescues empty). The fatal-state classification built on box-envelope replays measured the anchor parameterisation bug, not the board. Positions are same-episode-index, different boards: the trajectories diverge from step 0, so this is an episode-level comparison, not a same-state one.

The true-envelope c001-k1 trajectory terminates at a genuine dead end after 21 placements. Two independent instruments agree on the step-21 state: exhaustive generator enumeration returns 0 candidates for item 22, and the dense probe (2.5 cm lattice over the full cross-section, every support level, every orientation, geometric acceptance against the real half-spaces) returns 0 geometric hits. This is the same dense probe that overturned the previous dead-end certification with 16 counterexamples, so the failure mode of certifying from generator sampling alone does not apply here. Step 20 shows the approach: all 8 physically safe placements of item 21 are killers with all seven classes extinct and concentration 1.000 -- uniform annihilation, no choice matters. The episode then dies by the poison fixed-coordinate fallback on a board where nothing fits.
caveats: 2.5 cm lattice resolution; sub-lattice poses are not excluded

entries.claim: On the true-envelope c001-k1 trajectory the board-value collapse is non-gradual (total_slots 24 at step 18, 4-6 at step 19, 0 after step 20) and no measured step has a board-selection problem: within-step candidates are either all survivors (18, 19) or all killers (20), so discordant pairs are 0 everywhere and pairwise accuracy is undefined on the real search space just as it was on the artifact. Step 19 is the first state where features split within a step (total_slots 6 vs 4, concentration 0.333 vs 0.369) but all branches merge into the same uniform death at step 20, so the split has nothing to predict. Phi-as-within-step-tie-break is dead on the real space for this case; Phi(s) remains a state-level descriptor only (F1 flag-ON re-run: R/Hall moved on 16/43 snapshots, correlations stay weak, max |rho| 0.336). The premise that a value function can detect gradual impoverishment early is contradicted by the two-step cliff.

Horizon labels on the true-envelope c001-k1 trajectory refute 'no board-selection problem': at step 18 all 8 physically safe candidates carry byte-identical discrete features (total_slots 24, conc 0.080, extinct 2) yet their forward-played terminal depths split 20/21/23 -- the best branches (ranks 5,7, orientation 3) place +4 more items versus +1 for the worst, and every continuation still ends true_dead_end, so the depth difference is pure board quality. The live ranker is anti-correlated with the outcome: rank 0 (score 0.238) reaches 21 while the reached-23 branches score -0.44. At step 19 the split narrows to 20 vs 21, so step 18 is the decisive branching point. This supersedes the previous entry's 'the split has nothing to predict', which was asserted without horizon labels and conflated 1-step kills_stream survivorship with terminal depth. Consequences: (1) a selection problem exists on the real search space and is worth ~2-4 placed on this case; (2) candidate-derived discrete counts are confirmed blind to it (zero within-step variance at the branching step), which is the theory's stated reason for moving the observation unit to geometric pockets (TASK_C_BOARD_VALUE.md section 0.1); (3) the non-gradual collapse observation (24 -> 4-6 -> 0 slots) stands, but it describes the feature resolution, not the absence of choice.
caveats: forward play uses the live deadline-driven policy under measurement CPU load; depths are reproducible only in that environment

entries.claim: The 20/21/23 horizon split behind 'selection problem exists, worth 2-4 placed' was produced by a defective instrument and the claim is UNESTABLISHED. The Monte-Carlo rollout board value does not rank branches and is not promoted. v1 (support-level lattice scan, full rejection_reason) failed on magnitude: the shipped policy's placements are release drops settled by physics, so static support acceptance under-counted 6-12 achievable placements as 0-2, with the bias growing with clutter. v2 (5 cm heightmap drop accepted by release_rejection_reason) fixed the magnitude (3.4-5.9 vs measured 6-12) but not the ranking: on the step-10 labeled branches Spearman(mc, placed) = -0.344 (n=8, indistinguishable from zero), with the best branch (+12) scored mid-pack and one of the two worst (+6) scored highest. Per the pre-registered rule the line is closed: no ranking integration, no further rollout iterations. Caveats that bound the conclusion without reopening it: the validation label is the outcome on the single configured arrival stream while MC estimates the prior expectation -- these are different quantities and n=8 boards x 1 stream has no power to compare them; a proper validation would average continuations over sampled streams, whose cost is not justified by anything measured today. The v1->v2 magnitude fix stands as instrument knowledge: any future capacity estimate on settled boards must use release semantics, not static support acceptance.

entries.claim: The death-band lexicographic risk gate is the first intervention since the envelope fix to move placed upward.
